SARVARC Diagrams and Graphs: The Capability That Turns Raw Data Into a Client-Ready Chart

September 22, 2026

Most people building a report today are stuck moving between a spreadsheet app, a chart maker, a diagram tool, and a document editor, exporting and re-uploading at every step. SARVARC Workspace was built to remove that hopping entirely, and Diagrams and Graphs is the module that proves it.

It is not a standalone chart maker bolted onto the side of the product. It is a core capability that sits inside the same workspace where the data was built and the same workspace where the final report gets exported. Here is how it actually works, how it connects to everything else inside the platform, and why that connection is what makes a chart look genuinely professional in a finished report rather than pasted in. You can read more about the platform it lives inside on our Workspace overview.

Two Modes, One Module

Diagrams and Graphs is split into two clearly separated modes, sitting side by side so switching between them takes one click.

Data Charts is the canvas-based chart builder. It takes numbers and turns them into visuals, from the everyday bar, line, area, pie, and donut charts, through to more advanced formats built for real analytical work.

Flowchart/Diagram is a text-to-diagram engine, powered by what SARVARC calls FlowIQ, built on the Mermaid rendering engine. Type plain text describing a process, and it renders instantly as a flowchart, sequence diagram, org chart, mind map, or Gantt chart. No dragging boxes around a canvas and manually connecting arrows. Templates exist for each type so a person can start from a working flowchart, org chart, or Gantt chart and edit from there.

Inside this same mode sits Business Mind, which works differently from the other diagram templates. Instead of starting from a blank canvas, it reads whatever data is already loaded in Data Charts and automatically lays out the totals, the top and bottom performer, the trend direction, and a plain business takeaway as a ready-made mind map. It turns a table of numbers into a summary someone can actually read at a glance.

A Chart Library Built for Real Reporting, Not Just Basics

Data Charts goes well beyond the standard bar, line, and pie. The full list includes:

  • Bar, Grouped Bar, Line, Area, Pie, and Donut charts for everyday reporting
  • Stacked and Diverging Stacked Bar charts, useful for comparing categories that include both positive and negative values, such as sales against wastage or returns in one view
  • Tornado charts, built specifically for two-series side-by-side comparisons like Supplier A against Supplier B
  • Waterfall, Pareto, and Funnel charts for sequential or cumulative analysis
  • A full 3D suite: 3D Bar, 3D Grouped Bar, 3D Histogram, 3D Scatter, and 3D Box Plot charts, each rendered on its own canvas
  • A dedicated Map tab with a choropleth world map builder for country-by-country data, running on live map tiles

The 3D chart types also carry a Hologram mode, a glowing rendering style built specifically for them, along with the ability to record a rotating video of a 3D chart with an optional caption underneath. That turns a static chart into something a person can actually drop into a presentation, not just a document.

The chart type picker open on Pie Chart, with the rest of the library — Bar, Line, Waterfall, Funnel, Tornado, Pareto, and the 3D suite — listed right below it

Colour Palettes Built Like an Analyst's Toolkit

Colour choice sounds like a small detail until a chart goes in front of a client and looks thrown together. Data Charts ships six built-in palettes:

  • Vibrant, a bright, energetic default for general use
  • Professional, the module's default scheme: deep sapphire, champagne gold, wine, emerald, slate blue, bronze, plum, and teal, muted enough to sit together on one chart without clashing, but distinct enough that each series is still easy to tell apart. It reads like an analyst report or annual report chart rather than default software output.
  • Pastel, for softer, lighter presentations
  • Earth, a warm, muted, natural tone set
  • Ocean, a cool blue-to-orange gradient palette

A person can click any swatch to recolour an entire chart from that point, save custom colours to a personal swatch row for reuse, or lock every series to a single colour. Currency formatting is handled automatically too. The system detects which currency symbol was present in uploaded or pasted data and applies it on its own, only stepping back once someone manually sets a format.

The palette dropdown, with each named scheme listed for one-click switching

The Professional palette's swatch row, plus custom colour and Black/White options for fine-tuning any series

How It Connects to the Rest of the Workspace

This is the part that actually matters. A chart in SARVARC is never an isolated file sitting somewhere else.

Data can be built directly by uploading a CSV, Excel, TSV, TXT, or JSON file, with columns read and mapped automatically. But the more useful path runs through Data Arrangement, SARVARC's connected spreadsheet module. A table built there can be pushed into Diagrams and Graphs with a single click using a dedicated "Push to Diagrams" action on the table itself. Build the table once, and the chart is one click away, with no export or re-upload in between.

The same principle applies to data collected through SARVARC Forms. Responses collected in a form flow into the workspace's data layer rather than sitting locked inside the form tool, which means information gathered from clients or a team can end up feeding a chart in the same place it was collected, without ever leaving the platform.

For genuinely large datasets, a multi-chart suggestion system kicks in. When a wide or heavy upload comes in that looks like several comparable metrics tracked over the same categories, Diagrams and Graphs notices before a person has to. A popup lays out what it found — how many rows, how many numeric columns, how many columns total — and offers a short list of ways to handle it: a single grouped bar chart clustering the comparable columns together, one separate chart built per column, a "top entries plus an Other bucket" view for long tails, or simply the one chart already picked in the upload panel. Nothing is forced; a person picks the shape that fits the data.

Choosing "one chart per column" builds the full set at once — nine charts from nine metrics in the example below, each rendered as its own small chart — and drops them into a gallery strip beneath the chart canvas. Every chart in that strip stays clickable on its own, so clicking one swaps it into the main canvas to edit, rename, or restyle individually. A "Push all to Workspace" button on the same strip sends the entire set into a report in one action, which is the same multi-chart gallery push mentioned above for getting a finished set into Refine Report.

The module reads a wide upload, counts what it found, and offers a few ways to chart it — nothing is built without a choice

One upload, nine charts: click any one to edit it on its own, or push the whole set into the report at once

From Number to Narrative

One of the more distinctive pieces of this module is Written Analysis. It is opt-in, so nothing generates until it is asked for, but with one click, a plain paragraph analysis appears beneath the chart, describing what it shows in words instead of leaving a viewer to interpret the shape of some bars alone. Paired with a Growth % toggle, which can replot bar, line, and area charts as percentage change from the first value instead of raw numbers, a person can move from raw upload, to number, to shape, to written interpretation, all in the same panel.

Every chart also keeps a history. Saved charts sit in a dedicated dropdown, so earlier versions built while iterating on the same report stay available instead of being overwritten and lost.

Getting the Chart Into an Actual Professional Report

Once a chart or diagram is built, it does not need to be screenshotted or manually reinserted anywhere. It can be exported as a PDF, an embedded chart inside a DOCX file, a JPEG, a PNG, or a crisp 3840x2160 4K PNG for print or a fully zoomed map view. More importantly, it can be pushed directly into the Workspace document a person is already building, through a dedicated "Insert chart into Workspace" action, with an option to push every chart in a multi-chart gallery into the document at once.

This is where the connection to Refine Report closes the loop. A chart built in Diagrams and Graphs can land directly inside a document that then goes through the same formatting pass that makes every SARVARC report client-ready. The chart does not sit apart from the report as a separate asset someone has to place by hand. It becomes part of the same document, in the same formatting pass, ready to send.

A chart tool makes a picture. A connected workspace turns a table someone already built into a professional report someone can actually send.

A Practical Example

Picture a small business owner tracking quarterly sales across three regions. The numbers live in a table inside Data Arrangement, built or cleaned up there over a few weeks. Instead of exporting that table to a chart tool, they click "Push to Diagrams," land in Data Charts with the data already mapped, pick a Grouped Bar chart to compare regions side by side, apply the Professional palette so it reads like something from an annual report, and turn on Written Analysis so a plain paragraph explains which region is leading and by how much. From there, one click sends the finished chart straight into the Workspace document they are already building for the client, where it sits alongside the same formatting pass used by Refine Report. Nothing was exported, re-uploaded, or rebuilt from scratch at any step.

The same flow works if the numbers started life as client responses collected through SARVARC Forms instead of a manually built table. The data still lands in the same connected layer, and the chart-building process does not change.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Diagrams and Graphs a separate product from SARVARC Workspace?

No. It is a built-in module inside SARVARC Workspace, not a standalone app or a third-party integration. It shares the same account, the same data layer, and the same document canvas as every other module in the platform.

Can a chart be built from data that already exists in the workspace?

Yes. Tables built in Data Arrangement can be pushed into Diagrams and Graphs with one click through a dedicated "Push to Diagrams" action, and data collected through SARVARC Forms flows into the same data layer, so it can feed a chart without being re-entered anywhere.

What chart types does it support?

Bar, Grouped Bar, Line, Area, Pie, Donut, Stacked, Diverging Stacked Bar, Tornado, Waterfall, Pareto, and Funnel charts, plus a 3D suite covering Bar, Grouped Bar, Histogram, Scatter, and Box Plot, and a choropleth world map for country-by-country data.

Does it support diagrams and flowcharts, not just charts?

Yes. A separate Flowchart/Diagram mode, powered by FlowIQ, generates flowcharts, sequence diagrams, org charts, mind maps, and Gantt charts from plain text, with starter templates for each. Business Mind additionally builds a mind map directly from whatever data is already loaded in Data Charts.

Can a finished chart be inserted directly into a report?

Yes. A chart can be exported as PDF, DOCX, JPEG, PNG, or 4K PNG, or pushed directly into the Workspace document being built, using the same document that then goes through SARVARC's report formatting pass.

Why This Matters

Build a table in Data Arrangement, or collect it through Forms, push it into Diagrams and Graphs, pick from a real library of chart types and a genuinely considered set of colour palettes, add a written analysis if it helps, and drop the finished visual straight onto a client-facing document. All of that happens without exporting a single file in between or opening a second tool.

That is the same principle behind everything inside SARVARC Workspace: remove the friction between raw content and finished output, so the tool does the repetitive part and you do the part that matters.
